title: Locality-aware remap stencil for KV allocation and fragmentation mitigation
creator: Marco Nguyen
description:
Background:
The KV cache on GPU experiences slow fragmentation creep under real production workloads with mixed sequence lengths and bursty continuous batching. Existing slab and slot reclaim techniques reduce peak OOMs but cause steady-state throughput regressions due to excessive background compaction or high eviction churn.

Goal:
Design and implement a lightweight allocation/remap strategy (the "remap stencil") that: 1) preserves top-of-hot-request locality for continuous batching, 2) exposes low-cost, incremental defragmentation windows, and 3) minimizes background kernel overhead on critical inference paths.

Proposal summary:
- Introduce a thin virtual-to-physical segment remap layer (stencil) that allows live remapping of small contiguous virtual regions to physical microsegments without copying token KV blobs inline.
- Use access-pattern sketches (tiny per-segment hit counters and last-access timestamps) to compute a locality score. The remap controller favors coalescing high-locality segments into contiguous physical microsegments.
- Perform background remap operations opportunistically during inter-batch idle windows or during low-utilization scheduler slots to avoid impacting tail latency. Remap is an O(1) metadata update for most cases; copying occurs only when physical free space is unavailable.
- Add a gentle eviction token (soft-pin) for recently remapped segments so active batches do not race with compaction. Soft-pins time out quickly (milliseconds) to limit leakage.

Design details:
- Data structures: keep per-epoch microbitmap and a compact 16-bit locality score per virtual segment. Global free list is maintained as microsegment ranges to enable quick coalescing.
- Remap heuristics: schedule merges when contiguous free microsegment range >= target_window_size (configurable per-model), and prioritize segments with locality_score >= threshold.
- Integration with continuous batching: the batching runtime tags requests with sequence-length buckets; remap prioritization uses bucket-weighted locality to keep typical KV chains contiguous for common sequence-lengths.
- Safety: remap is first-class operation in the runtime with atomic pointer swap and epoch fencing. If copy is required, it runs on worker streams with priority low and exposes progress via trace points.

Telemetry & metrics to capture success:
- Fragmentation ratio (free microsegments / total microsegments) over time per model and per GPU.
- Tail latency P95/P99 during remap windows vs baseline.
- Background copy bandwidth and CPU/GPU cycles consumed by remap operations.
- Eviction churn (tokens evicted/sec) and remap success rate (remap performed without copy).
- Memory utilization delta before/after remap events.

Testing plan:
- Microbench: synthetic mix of short/long sequences with per-bucket mixes to validate locality score correlates with request locality.
- Scale test: multi-tenant inference pool with continuous batching to measure throughput, P99 latency, and steady-state memory fragmentation compared to current slab compactor.
- Fault injection: simulate interleaved remap and eviction to ensure no KV corruption and verify fencing semantics.

Rollout plan:
1) Implement remap controller behind a feature flag and default it off in hosted clusters.
2) Canary on dedicated nodes with non-critical workloads, enable only metadata-only remaps (no copies) initially.
3) Enable opportunistic copy remaps for selected models with low customer impact.
4) Gradually widen to production if metrics show reduced fragmentation ratio and no increase in P99 latency.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Config granularity: per-model vs global thresholds. We recommend per-model but default sensible global baseline to reduce config surface.
- Soft-pin timeout tuning: too long increases memory leakage, too short causes races. Need experiments to find sweet spot per batch size.
- Complexity vs benefit: additional metadata increases per-segment footprint; evaluate cost on smaller GPU memories (e.g., 24GB nodes).

References / artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/KV/Remap+Stencil+Design
- Initial benchmark PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/6241
- Experiment dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv-remap/kv-remap-canary

Success criteria:
- 30% reduction in fragmentation ratio for high-churn models within 48h of activation on canary nodes.
- No more than 5% regression in P99 latency during steady-state.
- Background copy utilization under 10% of GPU write bandwidth on average.
